description: One rule that says what a line on a bank statement is: if the description contains CHEVRON, this is Fuel and it books to 5200. Rules are DATA rather than code — a farm that starts buying from a new co-op adds a row, not a release. Nothing here posts anything: a rule fills in the category, the expense account and the party on a Bank Transaction, and a person or a Journal Entry still decides what to do with it. Rules are tried in priority order and the FIRST match wins, so a specific merchant rule belongs at a lower number than the generic word rule that would otherwise swallow it.
name: Bank Categorization Rule

fields.description: What this rule is called, for a person reading the list. Unique within the company — two rules with the same name are indistinguishable in the report that says which rule categorised a transaction.
fields.label: Rule Name

fields.description: The label a matching transaction is filed under — Fuel, Chemicals/Spray, Irrigation. Free text rather than a Select, deliberately: the categories a farm actually uses are the farm's business, and a fixed list would need a release every time one changed. Where a category matches an Expense Receipt category exactly, the two sides of the reconciliation line up on their own.
fields.label: Category

fields.description: A disabled rule is kept and skipped. Deleting a rule loses the record of why a year of transactions were categorised the way they were.
fields.label: Enabled

fields.description: Lower runs first, and the FIRST match wins. A specific merchant (CHEVRON, priority 10) belongs below the generic word (FUEL, priority 100) that would otherwise swallow it.
fields.label: Priority

fields.description: The GL account a matching transaction belongs in. OPTIONAL — a rule with a category and no account still sorts the statement, which is most of the value; it just cannot tell a Journal Entry where to post. Never guessed: a rule created without one comes back saying so.
fields.label: Expense Account

fields.description: Where the cost is booked below Company, if the operation tracks that.
fields.label: Cost Center

fields.description: The cost center for the BANK side of a posting, where an operation books its cash movements somewhere other than the cost they pay for. Separate from Cost Center because they are two different sides of one entry and a single field would make a transfer between two accounts land entirely on whichever one was named.
fields.label: Bank Cost Center

fields.description: Which field on the Bank Transaction the pattern is tested against. `description` is the memo line a bank feed writes and is what nearly every rule wants. IGNORED by the match types that name their own field — merchant_exact and merchant_contains read the merchant, description_regex reads the description, plaid_category_matches reads the feed's own category.
fields.label: Match Field

fields.description: How this rule decides. The first four compare `pattern` against `match_field`, case-insensitively. The rest name their own field so a rule reads as what it is: `merchant_exact` and `merchant_contains` test the MERCHANT (bank_party_name, falling back to the description where the feed left it empty); `description_regex` is a regular expression on the memo; `plaid_category_matches` tests the feed's own category and matches a prefix, so FOOD_AND_DRINK catches FOOD_AND_DRINK_RESTAURANTS; `amount_range` has no text at all and matches on the amount bounds alone; `combined` ANDs every criterion that is filled in. Direction and the amount bounds are ANDed onto EVERY match type — they are not a match type of their own, they are a gate on all of them. Every regular expression is compiled when the rule is saved, so one that would explode mid-run is refused here.
fields.label: Match Type
fields.options:
contains
starts_with
equals
regex
merchant_exact
merchant_contains
description_regex
plaid_category_matches
amount_range
combined

fields.description: The text to look for. Case-insensitive — bank feeds shout, and a rule that only matched CHEVRON would miss Chevron. Not required for `amount_range`, which has no text criterion, and optional on `combined`.
fields.label: Pattern

fields.description: The aggregator's own category, for `plaid_category_matches` and as one criterion of a `combined` rule. Matched as a PREFIX and case-insensitively, because these categories are hierarchical — TRANSPORTATION catches TRANSPORTATION_GAS, and a rule that had to name every leaf would be out of date the next time the taxonomy grew one.
fields.label: Plaid Category

fields.description: Whether this rule applies to money out, money in, or both. Most expense rules are Withdrawal: a refund from the same merchant is not the same category as a purchase from them, and matching it would file a credit as a cost.
fields.label: Direction

fields.description: Smallest absolute amount this rule applies to. Blank means no floor.
fields.label: Amount Min

fields.description: Largest absolute amount this rule applies to. Blank means no ceiling. A fuel-card rule capped at 2000 stops a wire transfer that happens to name the same vendor being filed as a tank of diesel.
fields.label: Amount Max

fields.description: OPTIONAL. When set, a matching transaction that names nobody gets this party — which is what makes a year of fuel totallable per vendor and what a 1099 pre-fill reads. A transaction that already names a party is never overwritten.
fields.label: Party Type

fields.description: The vendor's name as it should READ, for a transaction whose feed left `bank_party_name` empty. Not a Link and not a substitute for one: a name is what a person sees on a statement line, a Party is what a 1099 totals — a rule may set either, both, or neither, and neither is ever written over a value that is already there.
fields.label: Party Name

fields.description: How many transactions this rule has categorised. A rule at zero after a season is a rule whose pattern never matched anything — which is worth knowing before trusting the ones that did.
fields.label: Times Applied
